# A second-order condition for every selection of exact quantile covers

This note concerns an explicitly C2 finite body-parameter family in an OPEN
parameter neighborhood. An explicitly feasible C2 equality chart may be
used as the parameter family instead. It does not assert that arbitrary
attained mixed-depth extrema are smooth or lie on such a chart. Coincident
cap/body boundaries require a further second-order analysis, not present
here.

## 1. Exact second derivative of a circuit quantile cover

Use the exact covers of circuit-quantile-cover-variation.md. For a selected
active circuit c at index z, write

    F_j(p,b)=mu_p(H_j(b)),       S_j=-partial_b F_j>0,
    sum_j rho_j b_j=A.z,

with the ambient normals and positive circuit weights fixed. Assume each
F_j is C2 near its original cap and total mass M(p)>0 is C2. The anchor's
proper section gives S_j>0. The implicit-function theorem gives C2 roots
Q_j(p,tau) and the C2 common-mass root tau_c(p). These caps remain an EXACT
closed whole-fiber cover at every nearby p.

For a parameter direction delta put

    B_j=partial_p F_j[delta],
    theta_j=(rho_j/S_j)/(sum_k rho_k/S_k),
    a=tau_c'[delta]=sum_j theta_j B_j,
    v_j=(B_j-a)/S_j.

Here v_j is the first derivative of the jth adjusted threshold. Differentiating
F_j(p,Q_j(p,tau_c(p)))=tau_c(p) twice along the straight parameter line gives

    R_j=partial_pp F_j[delta,delta]
           +2 partial_pb F_j[delta] v_j
           +partial_bb F_j v_j^2,
    tau_c''[delta,delta]=sum_j theta_j R_j.                  (1)

Indeed the jth second derivative equation is tau_c''=R_j-S_j b_j'',
while differentiating the cover identity twice gives sum_j rho_j b_j''=0.
Multiply by rho_j/S_j and sum to obtain (1). Thus the reciprocal-section
weights persist at second order, and the curvature terms cannot be replaced
by the fixed-threshold cap Hessians alone.

Let f_c=tau_c/M, with f_c(p0)=beta. Its first gradient is

    g_c=(d tau_c-beta dM)/M.

On a direction delta with g_c(delta)=0, its Hessian simplifies to

    Q_c(delta)=[sum_j theta_j R_j-beta M''[delta,delta]]/M.   (2)

The normalization cross terms vanish exactly because tau_c'=beta M'.

## 2. A second-order alternative from actual covers

Select ANY one critical circuit for EACH globally deepest integer index;
retain slack circuit covers at the other indices. Write these selected
normalized comparison functions as f_1,...,f_k. They satisfy near p0

    actual maximum depth at p <= max_i f_i(p),
    f_i(p0)=beta.

Suppose p0 is an attained local minimum of actual depth. Put g_i=df_i(p0),
and let delta lie in their COMMON kernel. Write q_i=D2 f_i(p0)[delta,delta],
using (2) for each selected circuit. Then there exist numbers pi_i>=0,
summing to one, such that

    sum_i pi_i g_i=0,           sum_i pi_i q_i>=0.            (3)

Proof: if for some acceleration vector a all g_i(a)+q_i were negative,
the actual parameter path p(t)=p0+t delta+(t^2/2)a would give

    f_i(p(t))=beta+(t^2/2)[g_i(a)+q_i]+o(t^2)<beta

for every selected deepest circuit, and the nondeep covers would remain
strictly below beta. Their exact cover would contradict local minimality.
Therefore the affine subspace q+{(g_i(a))_i:a arbitrary} does not meet the
open negative orthant. Finite-dimensional separation gives a nonzero vector
pi>=0 annihilating every (g_i(a))_i and with pi.q>=0. Normalize its sum to
one. This is (3); no compactness of an unbounded acceleration search is used.

Equivalently, if B={pi>=0:sum pi=1,sum pi_i g_i=0}, then

    max_(pi in B) sum_i pi_i Q_i(delta) >=0                  (4)

for every common-kernel delta. The balanced weights may depend on delta.
It would be incorrect to select one convenient first-order balance and
assert its Hessian is positive semidefinite when B has multiple points.

## 3. The one-site and two-site conclusions

With one deepest site, the first-order quantile-cover condition already
gives g_1=0, for EVERY choice of its active circuit. Equation (3) says that
the Hessian of EVERY such normalized quantile comparison is positive
semidefinite on the whole parameter space.

With exactly two deepest sites, suppose for a given arbitrary circuit
selection the two gradients are nonzero. The first-order condition gives
g_2=-c g_1 for a unique c>0. The only normalized balance is

    pi1=c/(1+c),        pi2=1/(1+c).

Consequently the quadratic form

    [c Q_1(delta)+Q_2(delta)]/(1+c)                          (5)

is nonnegative on ker(g_1). This holds for EVERY selection of a circuit at
each of the two sites. A negative direction provides an actual improving
path: choose its acceleration to equalize the two second coefficients;
their common value is the negative expression (5).

If both gradients vanish, the correct statement is max(Q_1,Q_2)>=0; if
only one vanishes, the balancing weight can be supported on it. These
degeneracies are not covered by a claimed unique positive balance.

## 4. Relation to the rainbow rank lemma and limitations

The robust rank lemma identifies a low-dimensional span of all first
circuit gradients for an essential block. Formula (3) uses the actual
second derivatives on a common kernel, so it can distinguish configurations
which satisfy all first-order stresses. It supplies an explicit new test
using the cap derivatives (1), rather than another arbitrary one-cover
multiplier equation.

The circuits in (3) must still cover ALL globally deepest sites. A smaller
first-order essential block cannot simply replace that set at second order:
discarded deepest sites may prevent a descent even when their first-order
gradients were unnecessary. For the three-fiber model, the proved fact that
at most one endpoint can be deepest means that the actual deepest set has
at most two sites, so Sections2 and3 apply directly whenever the C2 chart
and transverse-cap hypotheses hold.

No numerical cap bound or automatic removal of active compatibility follows
from this necessary condition alone. Its current use is a rigorous
second-order obstruction test, with every comparison function an actual
nearby closed cap cover.
